text: You now have four kinds of automated checks from this chapter -- SAST, dependency scanning, DAST, and container image scanning. The tempting next step is to wire all four into CI and fail the build the moment any of them reports anything. In practice that fails within weeks. A scanner that blocks a merge over a Low-severity style finding teaches developers one lesson fast: this pipeline is noise, and the fastest way to ship is to find a way around it -- a suppression comment, a rushed disable-the-check pull request, or just ignoring red X marks.

The fix isn't fewer checks, it's a smarter gate. Every scanner reports a severity -- Critical, High, Medium, Low. A well-designed gate uses that to decide what actually blocks: Critical and High findings fail the build, because they represent real exploitable risk. Medium findings surface as a warning or a ticket for later triage, but don't stop the merge. Low findings just accumulate in a dashboard for periodic review. The loudest signal gets reserved for the findings that actually deserve it.

Turning a scanner on for the first time against an existing codebase usually surfaces a backlog of pre-existing issues that predate the gate. If the gate blocks on all of them immediately, every team's very next pull request fails for work that has nothing to do with it. The standard fix is a baseline: record what exists at rollout time, and configure the gate to fail only on new findings introduced after that point, while the old backlog gets triaged separately on its own timeline.

Here's a real gate reading severity from scan output: the pip-audit step never fails the job directly, it just writes a JSON report. A separate evaluation step reads that report, checks for critical or high findings, and exits with a failure only if it finds them -- printing a warning, but not blocking, for medium findings. That separation between scanning and deciding is what makes one severity policy apply consistently across every scanner in this chapter, even though each produces a different report format.

A gate's thresholds aren't a one-time decision. Teams revisit them as they learn which finding categories actually matter and which don't, and as scanners get noisier or quieter over time. The goal through every adjustment stays the same: developers should trust that a failed build means something real, so that when the gate does fire, they fix the problem instead of looking for a way around it.
